topic: learning differences / disability accommodations in admissions
speaker_role: current admissions officer (Donell Durham, director of Southeast admissions at Marist University) plus a college disability-support program director (Mandy Buckaloo, Auburn's SKILL program) and a high school college counselor (Aaron Leighton, the Howard School)
commercial_incentive: None evident for the admissions/counseling advice itself; Auburn's SKILL program is disclosed as a separate fee-based supplemental service (not the presenters selling admissions consulting)
key_insights: College accommodations (under ADA/Section 504) are access-focused, not success-focused like high school's IDEA coverage, and there's no resource teacher tracking assignments for you - the burden shifts entirely to the student to self-advocate each semester

Whether to disclose a neurodivergent diagnosis on the application is genuinely institution-specific: it can help explain an upward grade trend or connect a student to specialized programs, but at some schools admissions officers have denied students because the institution knew it couldn't adequately support them

Foreign language or math course waivers are read differently depending on how central that subject is to a given school's core requirements/identity; students should ask admissions directly and can request statistics on how many admitted students had exemptions

The admissions director recommends applying to about 5-7 schools total: 1-2 reach, 2-3 match, at least 1 near-certain safety applied to early, citing internal data that acceptance rates for individual applicants dropped once they applied to 10+ schools (down to 65%) due to less-tailored, 'copy-paste' applications

FERPA (passed 1974) means colleges will not share grades/attendance with parents by default, even if parents are paying, unless a signed release is on file - and even then some support programs still won't disclose grading/attendance info

Documentation requirements for accommodations vary widely by school and should be researched before applying/visiting; tour guides (undergrads) often don't know about disability services, so families should proactively schedule a separate meeting with the accessibility office
The ACT has historically offered more flexible accommodations (e.g., multi-day testing, automatic audio) than the SAT, though this varies by student and colleges do not care which test is submitted
The admissions director advises reframing a neurodivergent diagnosis as a strength/difference in essays rather than a deficit, since colleges actively want varied thinkers, not homogeneity
specific_numbers_or_facts: FERPA was passed in 1974 (per Mandy Buckaloo)
Recommended application list size: 5-7 schools; acceptance rate dropped to 65% for students applying to 10+ schools, per internal multi-year data cited by Aaron Leighton
Auburn's SKILL program is a supplemental fee-based one-on-one coaching service with a waitlist described as 'full' for the current and next terms
notable_or_distinctive: A real admissions director openly explains the case-by-case, sometimes contradictory calculus of disclosing a disability (can help or can hurt depending on institutional fit) and encourages students to directly ask admissions reps for disclosure/waiver statistics - a level of candor rarely offered in general admissions content.
reliability_notes: Panelists repeatedly caveat answers with 'it depends,' reflecting genuinely high institution-to-institution variability rather than universal rules; auto-caption transcript has minor garbling of names/terms (e.g., 'furpa' for FERPA, 'neurodeiverse' for neurodivergent) but content is otherwise clear and credible given panelists' stated professional roles.
